angle: When a museum deletes its wall labels, does the information actually disappear or just migrate — and does the deaf visitor end up in a more level room, or in a room whose default channel has quietly become speech (docents, tours, audio guides) with text demoted to atmosphere?
correction_moment: At the Cleveland Museum of Art in October, expecting the ArtLens app to be text's exile, she finds it hands her more written context than any wall ever did — resizable, captioned, in her pocket — and her thesis that digital migration equals demotion breaks against a screen that treats text as the primary channel for the first time in the building's history.
cross_cite: Against the position that the room itself — its acoustics, its docent murmur, its spatial address — is the primary political layer and the label only ever paper over it: if that's true, deleting wall text changes nothing, and the fight over labels is a fight over decoration; this piece has to test whether the label was the architecture or the apology.
opening_scene: In September 2025, Calder Gardens opened in Philadelphia without a single wall label, and called the absence a philosophy.
resisting_example: Christine Sun Kim, whose entire practice insists captions matter, spent 2021 replacing Manchester's public captions with subjective ones like 'the sound of anticipation' — a deaf artist rejecting the neutral informational label from inside deaf culture, choosing interpretation over the very institutional text this piece is tempted to defend.
